initial_presentation: A 10-year and eight-month-old boy was admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit for severe vomiting, convulsions, and coma. He was born full term via normal delivery and is the third child of healthy parents. The first child was premature and passed away at two months due to asphyxia, while the second child is 24 years old and healthy. The boy experienced his first symptoms 24 hours after birth, characterized by very poor oral intake. At one year old, he was treated for frequent convulsions with antiepileptic therapy, which was discontinued at age three when the severity of the attacks decreased. Despite this, convulsions continued to occur frequently up to age 10. Recently, he developed strabismus and vision loss in the right eye. He also exhibited significant intellectual development delay.

A 38-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of fever, accompanied by generalized weakness, fatigue, and loss of appetite. The patient also reported an increased craving for salt. Physical examination revealed pallor, mild jaundice, and pigmentation on the palms, knuckles, and oral mucosa. There was no family history of similar conditions. Upon admission, his vital signs were recorded as follows: blood pressure at 90/60 mm Hg, pulse rate at 76 beats per minute, and respiratory rate at 13 breaths per minute.

A 63-year-old woman reported experiencing leg tremor and instability while standing for the past 2 years. She had a history of angina 5 years ago and briefly used a calcium antagonist, with no history of mental illness or use of psychotropic drugs. During the physical examination, continuous trembling was observed in her lower limbs when standing, which ceased when she walked, sat, lay down, or leaned against a wall. Fine ripples were noted in the quadriceps muscles while standing, with no similar movements in other body parts. There were no signs of bradykinesia, muscle rigidity, or gait disturbances. Additionally, there were no indications of supranuclear gaze palsy, cerebellar signs, autonomic dysfunction, restless legs syndrome, or cognitive dysfunction. She did not exhibit REM sleep behavioral disorder or insomnia. Alcohol had no effect on the tremor, and there was no family history of tremor or parkinsonism.

A 60-year-old male presented with a growth over the glans penis for two months, accompanied by pain. There was no history of contact bleeding. The patient was not circumcised. He had noticed a swelling on the scrotum for the past six months. On examination, there was a 2 x 3 cm ulceroproliferative growth over the glans extending over the corona onto the shaft of the penis. The ulcer was fixed to the ventral aspect of the glans penis with induration proximally extending up to the mid-shaft of the penis. Bilateral inguinal lymph nodes were palpable, 3-4 on each side, 0.5 cm in size, firm and mobile in nature. The patient also had a right-sided primary vaginal hydrocele.

The patient is a 66-year-old male who does not smoke, has normal blood pressure, and does not have diabetes. He has experienced spontaneous blistering at areas of friction since early adolescence and has a history of difficulty swallowing. Physical examination showed he was underweight and pale. Skin examination identified multiple flaccid blisters containing hemorrhagic fluid on the shins, elbows, trunk, groins, and buttocks, along with atrophic scarring. Mucosal examination revealed erosions on the hard palate and enamel defects. There was also scarring alopecia with sparse hair on the scalp and partial loss of toenails.
A 60-year-old Caucasian male of British origin was admitted in September 2007 due to sudden onset of difficulty speaking and swallowing.

The patient is a 17-year-old male born to nonconsanguineous parents, presenting with hyperpigmented, rough streaks in a broad-band Blaschko-linear distribution. These skin lesions have been present since birth and have progressively extended to large areas on the right side of his body. No other family members have similar skin lesions or any cutaneous conditions. Physical examination revealed follicular hyperkeratosis across his entire body, more pronounced in the darker skin patches. On the scalp, there was an area of scarring alopecia with perifollicular erythema and follicular hyperkeratosis, displaying a tufted-like folliculitis pattern. The patient also exhibited clinodactyly of the fifth finger on both hands, more pronounced on the left side.

A 7-year-old boy from the countryside of Maranhão, northeastern Brazil, was admitted to the PICU with a 6-day history of fever, headache, vomiting, maculopapular rash, severe abdominal pain, conjunctival hyperemia, photophobia, raspberry tongue, hyperemia with lip desquamation, right cervical lymphadenomegaly, and edema. He also exhibited mild tachypnea without respiratory symptoms in normal room air. Upon admission, a fluorescence immunoassay for SARS-CoV-2 showed reagent immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies with titers >30.0 AU/mL (normal, <1.4 AU/mL) and nonreactive immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies with a titer of 0.1 AU (normal, <1.1 AU). The mother reported flu-like symptoms in the child one month prior.

A 43-year-old female office worker presented in 2020 with a 3-year history of headaches and over a year of cognitive issues. She had been experiencing migraines without aura since 2017, initially lasting a few minutes to half an hour, but progressively worsening in frequency and duration. After more than a year of headaches, she developed memory decline and slow cognitive responses, initially struggling with recall and later showing emotional indifference, abnormal communication, and reticence. She had no prior infectious illnesses. In her thirties, she experienced two ischemic strokes, resulting in slow movements and limb weakness. She also had lumbar spondylosis and lumbago for 5 years, with urinary retention occurring 6 months ago. Her low back pain varied in duration and intensity, sometimes requiring painkillers. She had thinning hair since childhood. There was no history of chronic diseases like hypertension, diabetes, or cardiovascular disorders. Her mother had moderate cerebral infarction and lumbar disc herniation, while her father, who was otherwise healthy, died suddenly in an accident. She has two healthy daughters. Upon admission, physical examination showed normal blood pressure and thinning hair, especially on the crown. There was a decline in response, calculation, and memory retention abilities.

The patient, a 22-year-old male from a family with no consanguinity, has healthy parents and an older sister. At age 15, he began experiencing cognitive difficulties, particularly with studying. By age 20, he exhibited a spastic-ataxic gait and developed slurred speech. Neurological examinations showed signs of cerebellar ataxia, increased muscle tension in the lower limbs, hyperreflexia in both upper and lower limbs, positive pathological reflexes, and ankle clonus, while muscle strength and volume remained normal.
